summary: In Arabic the words that point to a noun follow its gender and number: demonstratives (هٰذَا بَابٌ / هٰذِهِ غُرْفَةٌ), pronouns (الْبَابُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا / الْغُرْفَةُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا), person nouns used as predicates (هُوَ طَالِبٌ / هِيَ طَالِبَةٌ) — and, from lesson 16, adjectives and verbs. The great rule: plurals of things agree as feminine singular — هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ (these books), الْمَفَاتِيحُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا (the keys? they are here). Only plurals of people take plural agreement: هٰؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابٌ، هُمْ هُنَاكَ.

blocks.title: Things in the plural = “she”.
blocks.text: The most useful agreement rule of Arabic: any plural that is not people is treated like one feminine thing — هٰذِهِ، تِلْكَ، هِيَ, and later a feminine singular adjective and verb (الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ, the books are new).

blocks.title: People as predicates agree with the subject.
blocks.text: هُوَ طَالِبٌ، هِيَ طَالِبَةٌ، هُمْ طُلَّابٌ، هُنَّ طَالِبَاتٌ.

Coming later: an adjective follows its noun and agrees in gender, number, case and definiteness (الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ, the big house — lesson 16); a verb before its subject stays singular (كَانَ النَّاسُ أَصْدِقَاءَ).

askYourself: Which noun does the word refer to?
Is it a person, or a group of people?
Not people and plural? → feminine singular (هٰذِهِ، تِلْكَ، هِيَ).
People → masculine or feminine; one, two or several? (a mixed group is masculine)
Is the agreeing word a verb standing before its subject? → singular (later lessons).

traps: The gender comes from the word, not the thing: الْكَأْسُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا, but الْفِنْجَانُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا.
A mixed group of people is masculine: الطُّلَّابُ وَالطَّالِبَاتُ؟ هُمْ هُنَا.

quiz.why: Things in the plural → feminine singular.

quiz.q: الْكُتُبُ؟ … هُنَا. (The books? They are here.)
الطُّلَّابُ؟ … هُنَاكَ. (The students? They are there.)
quiz.why: People in the plural: masculine or mixed → هُمْ.

quiz.q: الْكَأْسُ؟ … هُنَا. (The glass? It is here.)

quiz.why: Things in the plural, far → تِلْكَ.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew agrees in gender and number the same way but gives plurals of things plural agreement (הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, these books) — switch the rule when you change language.
German agreement runs through articles and adjective endings in four cases (ein großes Haus); plurals of things are simply plural (die Bücher … sie).
Chinese has no agreement at all: 这本书 / 这些书 — only the measure word and 些 change.
